technical: The span-key comparison mixes two pipelines. The free check (Docker, console exporter) shows only old keys on default spans. The Splunk read on EKS shows default spans that also carry db.query.text, db.namespace and db.system.name. It is unknown which step adds them. Meanwhile the checklist tells readers that the preview 'carried db.query.text and db.system.name instead', which may be wrong for their data: if Splunk already holds those keys on default spans, readers could move their searches today. Fix: In one EKS run, set -Dotel.traces.exporter=otlp,console on one default pod, or add a debug exporter to the Collector's traces pipeline, and diff the agent's own keys against what Splunk APM returns for the same trace ID. Then credit the right component and rewrite the checklist item. If the new keys are already on default spans, say that span searches can switch to db.query.text and db.system.name now.

editorial: The opening's headline finding, db.namespace changing from 'postgres' to 'postgres|postgres', is never explained. The reader can't tell what the two parts mean, whether they change with schema settings, or how to write a filter that matches both before and after. Fix: Cite the database semantic conventions page that defines the PostgreSQL db.namespace format and state what each part is. Confirm it with one extra run that sets currentSchema in the JDBC URL. Then show a concrete Splunk APM filter or tag search that matches both forms during the migration.

editorial: Beyond the docs, the reader mainly gets confirmation of the documented ms-to-s change. The most actionable step, a chart or detector that reads the same in both units, is in the checklist but marked untested. Fix: Build it in the lab. Run a SignalFlow program that publishes the old use_time mean scaled by 0.001 next to the new metric over the same three round windows, then show the two lines or values agreeing within a stated tolerance. Then the reader can copy a demonstrated migration chart.

editorial: The screenshots come from a different, failed run than the one that produced the numbers in the post. Fix: Replace them with screenshots of the trace IDs printed in 05-fix.log (round 3 default and preview traces) from the passing run. If that isn't possible, put the run ID and date in each caption.

The pool series counts, the zero old-name series in the preview pair, load parity (19.89 rps, 0 errors) and the three per-round use_time ratios (989.4, 1009.7, 992.5) are corroborated in 04-reproduce.log and 05-fix.log. The config was captured per pod: same jar sha and printed env.

The span-key evidence comes from two different paths that don't agree. The Docker console check shows only old keys on default spans, but the default spans read from Splunk on EKS also carry db.query.text, db.namespace, db.system.name, db.operation.name and db.collection.name. The post discloses this but does not resolve it, and the checklist advice depends on it.
The screenshots come from an earlier EKS run that stopped on a Splunk read, not from the run that produced the numbers.
The '0.001 scaling' chart in the checklist was never built, and wait_time/create_time units were not read. Both are disclosed, but they remain untested advice.
The reader and decision are clear: a platform engineer deciding what to rename and convert in Splunk before 3.0. The title delivers what it promises.

Most results confirm what the OpenTelemetry blog already documents: the renames and the ms-to-s unit change. A ratio near 1000 is the expected result of that unit change. The one non-obvious finding, db.namespace becoming 'postgres|postgres', is in the opening but never explained, so the reader can't tell if it is stable or how to filter on both values.
The trade-offs are honest: what wasn't tested, the dual emission being off, and that the preview can still change. The logs look like a real session.
The structure is formulaic: TL;DR, 'Four things that changed', a checklist. The 112 operation.duration series is given with no breakdown of what it counts.
The BRIEF's demand evidence is weak: the project's own blog asks users to preview, but there is no search volume, reactions or views. That caps the score at 3.
The headline uses the words users would search ('OTel Java Agent 3.0', 'preview', 'one flag') and credits the product with the answer.
The timing is good if it publishes before 3.0 becomes the default.

claims.text: The OpenTelemetry project shipped 2.32.0 as the 3.0 release candidate and asks users to preview it now
The preview turns off dual emission for these names
The OpenTelemetry blog lists the code and messaging renames
The preview can still change before 3.0
Agent release v2.33.1 is the version used
Switching a live service in place would move its charts at once
Splunk stored values as sent, with no unit conversion
Plotting the old db.client.connections.* scaled by 0.001 makes both read in seconds
wait_time and create_time may also change unit (implied by 'check those on your own data')

brief.reader: Platform engineer running Java services on Kubernetes with the OTel Java agent and Splunk Observability Cloud
brief.decision: What to rename and convert in Splunk before the agent's 3.0 defaults arrive: pool metric names, pool timing units and database span keys
brief.question: What will OTel Java agent 3.0 change in the connection pool metrics and database spans I see in Splunk, and how can I see it before I upgrade?
brief.takeaway: One environment variable on the agent you already run shows 3.0's database names in Splunk today. Side by side with the default agent under the same load, the run shows which pool metrics and span keys get new names, and that the same pool timing is stored about 1000 times smaller because it is now in seconds, so any threshold written on the old values is worth checking.
brief.adds: The OpenTelemetry blog lists the renamed fields and the testing steps. This post runs both modes side by side on one live system and shows the result in Splunk: the pool metric names per service, the same pool timing stored in milliseconds and in seconds over three rounds, and every database key on real traces.
brief.open_question: With OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_COMMON_V3_PREVIEW=true alone on the same jar, running next to the default agent under the same load on EKS, which pool metric names does Splunk store per service, does any old name or old span key remain, and what is the ratio of the stored connection use time means in each of three rounds?
tradeoffs: The preview turns off the /dup dual emission for database, code and messaging, so old and new names are not sent side by side while it is on
The same pool timing is stored in seconds after the change, so anything built on the old millisecond values needs converting
The 2.33.1 preview can still change before 3.0, as the OpenTelemetry blog says
This run measures database pool metrics and database spans only; code and messaging renames are not measured
The preview pair uses its own deployment.environment so Splunk keeps the pairs apart; that label is the only other difference in the agent options
